newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa rand/bonds closing report.

text.p: The rand was coaxed back below the 4.50 level on Monday as perceptions grew that July 1 would not result in the currency gyrations some analysts have predicted.
The rand met little resistance on the way down, as local banks long of dollars and exporters stepped in line with London-based players and sold dollars for most of the day.
By 1410 GMT, the rand had firmed to 4.4985/5015 against the dollar from 4.5065/5095 late on Friday.
"There has been plenty of supply from everywhere...local and London," a trader said.
"It looks like the guys who were long waiting for foreign exchange controls have decided there is not going to be major pressure on the rand so they are lightening their positions," he added.

Dealers said that while the market remained wary of July 1, when South African individuals will be allowed to invest offshore for the first time, market participants were being put at ease by the armoury the Reserve Bank had assembled to defend the currency in the event of substantial capital flight.

Last week, the central bank announced it had arranged a $1.5 billion revolving credit facility. That came a day after the Finance Department announced it successfully launched a $500 million Yankee bond.
The central bank already has 21.8 billion rand as reserves, as well as access to offshore credit lines and reserves at local commercial banks estimated at some 15 billion rand.
"The feeling is that the Reserve Bank has enough in its armoury to prevent any excessive movements in the currency after July 1," another senior trader said.
"The market is setting itself up for something similar to when the financial rand was abolished...a non-event," a trader said.
Dealers said the local currency was expected to settle into a 4.4925 to 4.5100 range, while in the run-up to next Tuesday, they expected a 4.47 to 4.51 range.
Against the crosses, the rand was last trading at 25.6813/7206 yen from 25.4090/4269 on Friday, at 0.3828/3831 marks from 0.3838/3842 previously and at 7.4885/4980 against sterling from 7.4574/4653.
On the bond market, yields headed south mainly as a result of offshore buying on the back of the stronger rand, firmer U.S. Treasuries and softer money market rates.
The key R150 stock was last pegged at a 14.56 percent yield from 14.645 percent on Friday.
Dealers said volumes on the day were generally thin.
"The Reserve Bank have not been big sellers and local institutions have certainly not been selling so there has been a bit of a lack of supply," a trader said.
Profit-taking late in the day nudged yields off their intraday lows, they added.

Dealers said sentiment had received some support from improving conditions in the money market, where NCD rates were clipped by five basis points after the shortage fell to its lowest level in 12 months.
The Reserve Bank quoted the daily shortage at 5.389 billion rand on Saturday from 5.847 billion rand on Friday.

Roelf du Plooy, assistant general manager of the Reserve Bank's money and capital market division, said the shortage had fallen as a result of a 400 million rand decline in notes and coins, a mismatch in government flows as well as an effort to cater for coupon flows in August.

"We decided to transfer some money from the exchequer account to the Tax and Loan accounts at the banks in order for the government to earn interest on the money and to build up balances ahead of the huge coupon payments in August," he said.

In August, coupons of about eight billion rand have to be paid on a number of government stocks, notably the R150 and R153. "We have to build up the balances gradually from now onwards to handle those large payments," Du Plooy said.

Local commercial banks trimmed their three-month deposit rates to 16.00 percent offered from 16.05 percent on Friday, while the 90-day BA rate fell to between 15.40 and 15.60 percent from 15.45 to 15.60 percent before.
-- Paul Richardson, Johannesburg newsroom, +27 11 482-1003
